title: 1 Samuel 10:17–27
context: Samuel gathers the people to the LORD at Mizpah and reminds them that the LORD brought them out of Egypt and saved them from all their oppressors, yet they have rejected him by demanding a king. He presents them by tribes and families: Benjamin is taken, then the family of the Matrites, then Saul, who cannot be found until the LORD reveals that he is hiding among the baggage. Brought out, he stands taller than everyone, and Samuel presents him as the one the LORD has chosen; the people shout, “Long live the king!” Samuel records the regulations of the kingdom and sends the people home. The army, men whose hearts God had touched, goes with Saul to Gibeah, while worthless fellows despise him, and he holds his peace. Both traditions see God choosing publicly while the people’s rejection of him is named plainly.

verses.text: Samuel called the people together to the LORD to Mizpah;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Samuel calls the people together to the LORD at Mizpah, the place of earlier repentance and deliverance (1 Samuel 7:5–12). The setting invites the people to remember God’s past faithfulness as they receive the king they asked for.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the assembly is gathered “to the LORD,” framing the choice of the king as an act before God. Mizpah recalls the LORD’s victory in chapter 7, a reminder of who has truly saved Israel, as both traditions emphasize.

verses.text: and he said to the children of Israel, “The LORD, the God of Israel, says ‘I brought Israel up out of Egypt and I delivered you out of the hand of the Egyptians, and out of the hand of all the kingdoms that oppressed you.’
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note Samuel’s recital of God’s saving acts: bringing Israel out of Egypt and delivering them from all who oppressed them. God’s faithfulness is the backdrop against which the people’s choice is measured, and it calls them to grateful trust.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the recital of the exodus and later deliverances as a covenant reminder. God’s past grace establishes his claim on Israel, and the people’s request must be understood in light of all he has already done for them.

verses.text: But you have today rejected your God, who himself saves you out of all your calamities and your distresses; and you have said to him, ‘No! Set a king over us!’ Now therefore present yourselves before the LORD by your tribes and by your thousands.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note Samuel’s blunt charge that the people have rejected their God who saves them. They chose this path freely, and God still proceeds with the selection, showing patience with his people while making clear the seriousness of what they have done.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the people’s demand is called a rejection of the God who himself saves them, yet God directs the selection that follows. Human sin is named plainly while God’s rule continues unbroken, a combination both traditions recognize in the passage.

verses.text: So Samuel brought all the tribes of Israel near, and the tribe of Benjamin was chosen.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the tribe of Benjamin is chosen as the tribes are brought near. The process is public and orderly, confirming before all Israel what had been privately revealed, so that no one can say the choice was merely Samuel’s preference.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the selection likely proceeded by lot, though the text does not name the method, and see it as a means by which God makes his choice known (compare Proverbs 16:33). The selection of Benjamin publicly confirms the private anointing and shows that the outcome rests with the LORD.

verses.text: He brought the tribe of Benjamin near by their families and the family of the Matrites was chosen. Then Saul the son of Kish was chosen; but when they looked for him, he could not be found.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the striking moment when Saul, chosen, cannot be found. His hiding may reflect fear or reluctance, and it shows that God’s call does not override human feelings; Saul must still come forward and accept the role publicly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the process narrows from Benjamin to the Matrites to Saul, demonstrating God’s precise choice. Saul’s absence at the moment of selection underscores that the initiative is God’s, though readers in both traditions differ on whether the hiding signals humility or timidity.

verses.text: Therefore they asked of the LORD further, “Is there yet a man to come here?” The LORD answered, “Behold, he has hidden himself among the baggage.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that when Saul is missing, the people ask the LORD further and he answers. God engages with his people’s questions in real time, revealing that Saul has hidden himself among the baggage in a scene that is both humbling and almost comic.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that God himself reveals where Saul is hiding. The one the LORD has chosen cannot escape the choice, and the scene shows that the LORD, not Saul’s willingness or the people’s search, brings the matter to completion.

verses.text: They ran and got him there. When he stood among the people, he was higher than any of the people from his shoulders and upward.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that when Saul stands among the people he is taller than all of them from his shoulders upward. His appearance matches popular expectations of a king, which fits the people’s request, though the story will test whether his character matches his stature.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the repetition of Saul’s height from 9:2. He looks the part of the king the people wanted, and the narrator’s emphasis on outward appearance prepares for the later contrast with David, whom the LORD chooses by looking on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7).

verses.text: Samuel said to all the people, “Do you see him whom the LORD has chosen, that there is no one like him among all the people?” All the people shouted and said, “Long live the king!”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note Samuel’s presentation of Saul as the one “whom the LORD has chosen” and the people’s glad shout. The people accept the king God has given in answer to their request, and their acclamation is a genuine and public act of acceptance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that Samuel presents Saul as the LORD’s choice, not merely the people’s. The acclamation “Long live the king!” is real, yet the king remains under God, a theme the regulations recorded in the next verse will reinforce.

verses.text: Then Samuel told the people the regulations of the kingdom, and wrote it in a book and laid it up before the LORD. Samuel sent all the people away, every man to his house.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Samuel tells the people the regulations of the kingdom and writes them in a book laid up before the LORD. The king and people alike are placed under a written standard, so that the new arrangement is bound by accountability to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the written regulations a reflection of the law of the king (Deuteronomy 17:18–20), though the text does not say exactly what Samuel wrote. Laying the book up before the LORD signals that kingship in Israel is to be governed by God’s covenant order.

verses.text: Saul also went to his house in Gibeah; and the army went with him, whose hearts God had touched.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the army goes with Saul to Gibeah, men “whose hearts God had touched.” God moves people’s hearts to support his chosen leader, working through and with their willing response rather than against it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the narrator attributes the men’s loyalty to God touching their hearts. God not only chooses the king but also gives him followers, inclining human hearts toward his purpose, a point both traditions affirm while describing the mode of God’s working differently.

verses.text: But certain worthless fellows said, “How could this man save us?” They despised him, and brought him no tribute. But he held his peace.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that some worthless fellows despise Saul and refuse to bring tribute, asking how this man could save them. Not everyone accepts God’s choice, and Saul’s decision to hold his peace shows restraint at the start of his reign.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the scoffers’ question, “How could this man save us?” will be answered in chapter 11 when God gives Saul victory. Saul’s silence in the face of contempt is presented as fitting restraint, and both traditions see it as a promising beginning to his kingship.
